Franc, of France, who is sometimes called William the Frenchman. He founded a school in Geneva, in 1541. It is one of the oldest tunes in the books, and has been used throughout Christendom for over 300 years.

103.title: Clamanda
103.firstLine: Say, now, ye lovely social band,
103.scriptureReference: "If the Lord delight in us, then he will bring us into this land, and give it to us."—Num. 14:8
103.historicalNote: This tune is on page 42 of the 'Sacred Harp' as it was published in 1844. We have been unable to find any trace of its history or the words in the tune.

104.title: Greenfield
104.firstLine: How tedious and tasteless the hours
104.scriptureReference: "Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth I desire beside thee."—Ps. 73:25. "The presence of Christ affords delight."—Acts 13:25.
104.historicalNote: This widely-popular hymn, on 'Delights in Christ,' was taken from 'Olney Hymns,' in 1779. John Newton was one of the best English hymn writers. Born 1725 and died 1807; belonged to the Church of England. Louis Edson was born 1748 and died 1820. He was an American, and wrote some very valuable music. If he had never written any other tune but 'Greenfield' it would stand as a monument to his name throughout all ages.

105.title: The Lovely Story
105.firstLine: A story most lovely I'll tell,
105.scriptureReference: "Now is my soul troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour."—Jno. 12:25
105.historicalNote: It is not known whether Professor E. J. King composed or rearranged the words to the above tune. He was a fine singer, taught music in many counties of Georgia, and wrote some acceptable hymns and tunes.

106.title: Ecstasy
106.scriptureReference: "They shall be satisfied abundantly with the fatness of thy house: and thou shalt make them drink of the river of thy pleasure."—Ps. 36:8
106.historicalNote: The words are the two last verses of 'O When Shall I See Jesus?' by Rev. John Leland (1754-1844), a Baptist minister and friend of Thomas Jefferson. 'Ecstasy' is supposed to have been composed by T. W. Carter before the first revision of the 'Sacred Harp,' in 1844 or 1845.

107.title: Present Joys
107.firstLine: We thank the Lord of heav'n and earth,
107.historicalNote: See sketch of A. M. Cagle under tune, 'New Jordan.'

108.title: Let Us Sing
108.firstLine: Shall we ever meet again at the house,
108.scriptureReference: "Meet in 'a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.'"—2 Cor. 5:1
108.historicalNote: W. F. Moore was the first President of the Tallapoosa Singing Convention in 1867 and 1878. He composed several songs in the 'Sacred Harp.' This song is partly the melody of the old tune, 'Let Us Walk in the Light of God.'

109.title: Return Again
109.scriptureReference: "Wilt thou not revive us again that the people may rejoice in thee?"—Ps. 85:6
109.historicalNote: The original title was 'Prayer For Revival,' appearing in Olney's collection. Rev. William Williams (1717-1781), a Welsh preacher and medical doctor. John Newton (1725-1807) belonged to the Church of England.

110.title: Cleburne
110.firstLine: All hail the pow'r of Jesus' name,
110.scriptureReference: "A royal diadem in the hands of God."—Isa. 62:3
110.historicalNote: This great hymn was written by Rev. Edward Perronet about 1779. Professor S. M. Denson resides in Winston County, Ala. He has been teaching music for nearly forty years, and has composed a large number of hymns and tunes in this book, including: 'Heavenly King,' 'Camp-meeting Song,' 'The Great Provider,' 'Arbacoochee,' 'Tentha,' 'The Life Boat,' 'Glorious Day,' 'Gone to Rest,' 'Home in Heaven,' 'Jester,' 'Mt. Pisgah,' 'McKay,' 'Casander,' 'Consolation,' 'Cagle,' 'Winston,' 'Pilgrim's Hope,' 'Rejoice,' and 'Cullman.'

111.title: Praise the Saviour's Name
111.firstLine: Awake, ye saints, and sing the song
111.scriptureReference: "Sing unto the Lord a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth."—Isa. 41:10
111.historicalNote: Professor J. G. Land, the author of the above music and words, lives in Alabama.

112.title: The Great Provider
112.firstLine: Peace, troubled soul, thou need not fear,
112.scriptureReference: "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you."—Matt. 6:33
112.historicalNote: First published in the author's hymn book, on 'Grace, Faith and Repentance.' Composed before the nineteenth century; used in 1806 by Rev. James Haxley in Louisiana.

113.title: McKay
113.scriptureReference: "And he showed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and the Lamb."—Rev. 22:1
113.historicalNote: Second and third verse of 'On Jordan's Stormy Banks I Stand,' named 'Promised Land' in 'Rippan's Selection.' Author born 1727, died 1795. (In honor of Rev. S. M. McKay, of Clay County, Alabama.)

114.title: Gone To Rest
114.firstLine: Death has been here and borne away
114.scriptureReference: "Be faithful unto death and I will give thee a crown of life."—Rev. 2:10
114.historicalNote: Composed by Professor Denson in memory of his niece, Miss Delia Denson, who died April 4, 1908. (Footnote: Use father, mother, or brother, to suit.)

115t.title: Cagle
115t.firstLine: Hark! my soul, it is the Lord,
115t.scriptureReference: "For I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance."—Matt. 9:13
115t.historicalNote: William Cowper (1731-1800). See remarks about Mr. Denson on page 130.

115b.title: Winston
115b.firstLine: Jesus, I my cross have taken,
115b.scriptureReference: "Let him deny himself, take up his cross and follow me."—Matt. 16:24
115b.historicalNote: Henry Francis Lyte, a clergyman of the Church of England, born 1793, ordained 1818, died 1847.

116t.title: The Pilgrim's Hope
116t.firstLine: Why should we start and fear to die,
116t.scriptureReference: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord."—Rev. 14:13
116t.historicalNote: Original title 'Christ's Presence Makes Death Easy.' Watts born 1674, died 1748.

116b.title: Rejoice
116b.firstLine: Shepherds, rejoice, lift up your eyes
116b.scriptureReference: "Our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant."—Heb. 13:20
116b.historicalNote: Words taken from the 'Sacred Harp,' tune of 'Oxford,' page 306.

117.title: Casander
117.firstLine: Hosanna to Jesus, my soul's filled with praises,
117.scriptureReference: "I will sing praises unto my God while I have any being."—Ps. 146:2
117.historicalNote: Professor W. T. Power composed the original hymn in 1850; changed by Professor Denson in 1908. See sketch of Mr. Power under 'Royal Band.'

118.title: Home In Heaven
118.firstLine: There is a home in heav'n for me,
118.scriptureReference: "We have a building of God, an house, not made with hands, eternal in the heavens."—2 Cor. 5:1
118.historicalNote: Words to this tune are by C. H. Gabriel.

119.title: Consolation
119.firstLine: I know that my Redeemer lives
119.scriptureReference: "And being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him."—Heb. 5:9
119.historicalNote: First published in 'Medley's Hymns' in 1800; originally nine stanzas, changed by Professor Denson to suit the tune. Medley, a Baptist minister, born England 1739, died 1799.

120t.title: Cullman
120t.firstLine: When Paul was parted from his sins
120t.scriptureReference: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes."—Rev. 7:17
120t.historicalNote: Named for the County of Cullman, Ala., when Professor Denson first settled in Alabama after leaving Georgia.

120b.title: Sidney
120b.firstLine: My Shepherd will supply my need,
120b.scriptureReference: "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for his sheep."—John 10:11
120b.historicalNote: Words arranged by H. A. Paris. Both reside in Alabama.

121.title: Jester
121.firstLine: If our fathers want to go,
121.scriptureReference: "How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation."—Heb. 2:3
121.historicalNote: Composed by Professor Denson in their present shape. (In honor of Professor N. D. Jester, of Franklin County, Ala. Footnote: Use mothers, brothers, or sisters for both verses.)

122.title: Baptismal Anthem
122.firstLine: In those days came John the Baptist, preaching in the wilderness of Judea,
122.historicalNote: B. F. White was born in Spartanburg, S. C., 1800, and died in Atlanta, Ga., 1879. He married a Miss Golightly in 1825; moved from Spartanburg to Hamilton, Harris County, Ga., in 1842. He was a strict member of the Missionary Baptist church for almost all his life. He first compiled the 'Sacred Harp' and 'Tune Book of Sacred Songs' in 1844. It is claimed that Major White and his brother-in-law, William Walker, wrote the 'Southern Harmony,' and that Walker deprived White of credit for it, causing them to become estranged; White then moved to Georgia and brought out the 'Sacred Harp,' revised in 1850, 1859, and 1869, with 480 pages at present. Major White organized the Southern Musical Convention, and was president from that time until 1862, and again in 1867; the convention is still in existence. All tunes in the 'Sacred Harp' not composed by White were examined and corrected by him. He was self-taught in music. He was for several years connected with the county affairs of Harris County, Ga., holding the office of Clerk of the Superior Court, and also published a newspaper there called the 'Organ.' A full sketch of Major White's life, family, and the music book he wrote can be found in a brief history of the 'Sacred Harp,' compiled by J. S. James in 1904.

124.title: Parting Hand
124.firstLine: My Christian friends, in bonds of love,
124.scriptureReference: "But as touching brotherly love ye need not that I write unto you, for ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another."—1 Thess. 4:9
124.historicalNote: Jeremiah Ingalls was a native of Massachusetts, born 1764 and died 1828. In 1804 he published a book called 'Christian Harmony.' 'Parting Hand' was composed a year before that. He was a music teacher, traveling through New Hampshire, Vermont, and Massachusetts. Among his leading tunes are 'Northfield' and 'New Jerusalem.' It may be that Ingalls wrote the words as well as composed the music, as he usually wrote the words to his own tunes.

125.title: Journey Home
125.firstLine: O who will come and go with me?
125.scriptureReference: "A house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens."—2 Cor. 5:1
125.historicalNote: R. F. M. Mann was said to have had a very strong voice, a good singer and music teacher. He was a Georgian, living near Milledgeville, where he died several years ago, diseased in body and mind. He was a member of the Methodist church, and also of the Southern Musical Convention and the Chattahoochee Musical Convention. He has seventeen tunes credited to him in the 'Sacred Harp.'

126.title: Waldin
126.firstLine: Bless, O my soul, the living God,
126.scriptureReference: "Blessing for his goodness to the soul and body."—Ps. 103:1-7
126.historicalNote: This tune was composed in 1882 and published in the December (1883) Number of the 'Musical Million,' by Professor A. J. Showalter, who was at that time correcting harmony for Adline S. Kieffer, editor of the paper. Professor Bryan was born in Newton County, Ga., 1861, educated in the common schools of that county, finally completing his musical education at Emory College under the late R. M. McIntosh, in 1887. He has composed nearly twelve hundred gospel and Sunday school songs. He married Miss Mamie Johnson, and is at present living in Atlanta, Ga.

127.title: The Royal Band
127.firstLine: Hosanna to Jesus, my soul's filled with praises,
127.scriptureReference: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest."—Matt. 21:9
127.historicalNote: Little is known of W. T. Power. He was a member of the Southern Musical Convention for several years, and also a member of the Chattahoochee Singing Convention. He only composed this one tune and hymn, so far as can be ascertained. He was a teacher, and taught music in and around Georgia and Alabama for several years.

128.title: The Promised Land
128.firstLine: On Jordan's stormy banks I stand,
128.scriptureReference: "Thine eyes shall behold the King in his beauty: they shall behold the land that is very far off."—Isa. 33:17
128.historicalNote: Samuel Stennett was one of the most influential and highly respected ministers of the Dissenting persuasion in England, and a confidant of many distinguished statesmen of his time. Doctor of Divinity was bestowed on him by Aberdeen University. He composed and published thirty-eight hymns, and died in London in 1795. This tune is credited to Miss M. Durham in the 'Sacred Harp.' We have been unable to find out anything about her, or whether she made changes in the tune for the 'Sacred Harp.' The melody can be traced back for over one hundred years.

129.title: Rock of Ages, Dear to Me
129.firstLine: Rock of ages, dear to me,
129.historicalNote: Professor J. C. Brown is a son of S. M. Brown, who composed a great deal of music during his lifetime. He has composed music for several years and written many hymns. He has lived in Haralson County, Ga., a greater part of his life, but at present (1909) lives at Buchanan, Ga. He is quite feeble, and has been afflicted for several years. The words in this hymn have been re-arranged by Professor Brown; the original words were composed by Augustus Toplady in 1776. See page 6 of this book.

130t.title: Prayer of Saints
130t.firstLine: O blessed Saviour, hear our pray'r,
130t.scriptureReference: "Whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved."—Acts 2:21
130t.historicalNote: See sketch of Mr. Brown on page 129.

130b.title: Jesus Is Mine
130b.scriptureReference: "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and thou shalt be saved."—Acts 16:31
130b.historicalNote: Words re-arranged by Mr. Brown. See sketch on page 129.

131.title: Praise His Name for Evermore
131.firstLine: Let us sing our joyful lays
131.scriptureReference: "And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto God."—Ps. 40:3
131.historicalNote: F. C. Perry and J. C. Perry are connected with the Perry Brothers Music Company, publishers, of Chattanooga, Tenn., and Waco, Texas. They published a song book called 'Uplifting Songs,' by F. Clark Perry, James B. Harris, J. A. McPhail and W. L. Conaway, as well as other publications scattered throughout the country. F. C. Perry and J. C. Perry are ready music writers, and have their songs and tunes in a large number of music books.

132.title: After This Manner Pray Ye
132.firstLine: After this manner therefore pray ye:
132.historicalNote: The words of the above anthem are taken from the ninth verse of the sixth chapter of Matthew, which words were used by Christ in directing His disciples how to pray, and following these words is what is called the 'Lord's Prayer.' Professor G. B. Daniell has composed and written the words of several tunes; this anthem and one other, 'Home in Glory,' printed elsewhere in this book, are two of his tunes, composed in 1908. He has successfully taught singing schools at intervals for some time, and was one of the original organizers of the United Sacred Harp Musical Association. He does not follow music as an occupation, but labors for a living to support his family. He is one of the committee engaged in the revision of B. F. White's 'Sacred Harp.' He lives at present in Atlanta, Ga., and is a member and clerk of the Primitive Baptist church in that city. Mr. Daniell is 48 years of age, and belongs to a very numerous and influential family, a number of whom reside in Georgia and other States. Seven of his grandfather's brothers were Primitive Baptist ministers.

134.title: The Beautiful Home In Glory
134.firstLine: Jesus, my all, to heav'n is gone,
134.historicalNote: This hymn, 'Jesus, my all to heaven is gone,' was written by John Cennick, and is found in the author's 'Sacred Hymns,' 1743, under the title, 'Following Christ, the Sinner's Way to God.' There have been several changes in some of the verses since it was composed, or additions to the words, which were composed by Professor Daniell, 'To that home, that beautiful home in glory.' The chorus was composed in 1908, the time of the composition of the music. See sketch of Mr. Daniell under tune 'After This Manner Pray Ye,' on page 133.

135.title: Olney
135.firstLine: Come, Thou Fount of ev'ry blessing,
135.scriptureReference: "The fountain is Christ."—Zek. 13:1. "We shall receive the blessings from the Lord, and righteousness from the God of his salvation."—Ps. 24:5
135.historicalNote: Chopin was born in 1809 and died 1849. He was one of the great masters of music. His last words were said to his attending physician, 'Now my death struggle begins.' He remained conscious to the last, and added, 'God shows man rare favor when He reveals to him the moment of the approach of his death. This He shows me—do not disturb me.' John Robinson was born in Norfolk, Eng., 1735, and left an orphan. He was converted under preaching of Whitfield, and ordained to the Methodist ministry. He later joined the Baptist, then the Independent, and finally became a Unitarian. He died 1790.

136.title: Humble Sinner
136.firstLine: Come, humble sinner, in whose breast
136.historicalNote: Edmund Jones was a minister in the English Baptist church. He was born in 1721 and died in 1765. He composed a large number of hymns. The above is considered one of his best. Mr. Wall lives at this time (1908) in North Alabama. He is active in the cause of music, and has done much valuable work to advance the same.

137t.title: Farewell To All
137t.firstLine: And now, my friends, both old and young,
137t.historicalNote: Professor J. P. Reese composed a large number of tunes in the 'Sacred Harp,' as well as in many other books. He was also a correspondent for musical journals and secular papers. He was born, 1828 in Jasper County, Ga., and died at his home, near Newnan, 1900. He was buried in Oak Hill Cemetery, Newnan. An extended history of him is given in James' 'History of the Sacred Harp,' pages 94 to 99; also on page 69 in this book.

137b.title: Balerma
137b.firstLine: There is a land of pure delight,
137b.scriptureReference: "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes."—Deut. 34:4
137b.historicalNote: The original title to this hymn was 'Prospect of Heaven Makes Death Easy.' It was written by the author at his home in Southampton, while sitting at a parlor window, looking over the waters and beautiful scenery. It is claimed that the view across Southampton's waters, in the direction of the Bundant, Isles of Wight, is suggesting in its exquisite imagery of the fair land of the beyond. This hymn also suggests the leading of the children of Israel to the banks of the river Jordan. Robert Simpson was born in 1792 and died in 1832. He was a Scotchman, and composed a great many valuable tunes. See sketch of B. F. White on page 122.

138.title: Arbacoochee
138.firstLine: Behold the love, the generous love,
138.historicalNote: The words in this tune are the same as those in the tune 'Sardinia,' in B. F. White's 'Sacred Harp,' on page 296. The words are great favorites of Wyley J. James, who resides in Tallapoosa, Ga., and who is a great admirer of the old sacred songs. See sketch of Professor Denson on page 110.

139.title: Fillmore
139.firstLine: Great God, let all my tuneful pow'rs awake
139.scriptureReference: "I will sing unto the Lord as long as I live."—Ps. 114:33
139.historicalNote: John P. Rees, the author of this tune, was born in Jasper County, Ga., 1828, and died in Newnan, Ga. 1900. He was President of the Chattahoochee Singing Convention and President of the Southern Musical Convention for years. He composed a large number of sacred tunes, which were published in different books. He composed a large number of tunes and intended to compile a book, but died without doing so. He helped to revise the 'Sacred Harp' twice, and has a large number of tunes composed by himself in that book. 'Fillmore' is a stirring song, and is greatly enjoyed in conventions and singing societies.

141.title: The Bright Forever
141.firstLine: There's a sweet, a bright forever
141.scriptureReference: "So he bringeth them unto their desired haven."—Ps. 107:30
141.historicalNote: Professor Chas. Edw. Pollock is a ready composer, and is said to be a fine director of music. He has written a great many valuable hymns and tunes. He often writes his own hymns. His music is found in many of the hymn and tune books for the past few years. A glance at his music wherever seen readily convinces one that he is an able composer. The tune, 'The Bright Forever,' measures up to the usual order of this gifted musician. He is an American composer, mostly of Sunday school and church music. He was born in 1853.

142.title: Pleyel's Hymn (Second)
142.firstLine: While Thee I seek, protecting Pow'r,
142.scriptureReference: "Power belongeth unto God; also unto thee, O Lord, belongeth mercy; for thou renderest to every man according to his work."—Ps. 62:11,12
142.historicalNote: The author of this hymn wrote two volumes of poetry in 1786, which were published about that time. There were three verses in place of two in the original hymn, from which these two are taken. Miss Williams was born in England in 1762. Her poems were published when she was twenty-one years old. She visited Paris in 1788, at a period of great trouble, war being waged between England and France at that time. She was arrested on suspicion of being a foreigner, and an advocate of the Girondist cause, and imprisoned. She was not released until 1794. From this time until her death she lived partly in England, but mostly in France, and died in Paris in 1827. She composed this hymn while in prison. Ignaz Joseph Pleyel, author of the foregoing music, was born in 1757 and died in 1831 in Paris. He was the twenty-fourth child of a village school-master. He commenced the study of music when very young. He studied under Haydn, who often spoke of him as his best and dearest pupil. He was reared in Austria, and composed a great deal of music, and stood high as a musician.

143.title: Idumea
143.firstLine: And am I born to die?
143.scriptureReference: "A time to be born, and a time to die."—Eccl. 3:2
143.historicalNote: The original title to these words was 'And Others of Riper Years.' Charles Wesley composed over 6,000 hymns, and this one was among his favorite hymns. No trace can be found of A. Davidson, author of the music.

144.title: Heavenly King
144.scriptureReference: "To God only wise, be glory through Jesus Christ forever."—Rom. 16:27
144.historicalNote: The above hymn was first published in 1742. Some changes in the words have been made. It originally had twelve stanzas. John Cennick also composed other hymns, one of them being, 'Jesus, My All to Heaven is Gone.' He was born in 1718 and died in 1755; was a Methodist minister. See sketch of Professor Denson on page 110.

145.title: Sweet Affliction
145.scriptureReference: "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer: I have overcome the world."—John 16:33
145.historicalNote: The original name of the above tune was 'Greenville.' It was composed by John J. Rosseau. It is said that the tune was originally 'Love Serenade,' written about 1752. It was commonly known for a long time as 'Rosseau's Dream.' He was an unbelieving philosopher, musician and misguided moralist. It is claimed that he heard the melody of this tune in his dreams, and it was sung by a legion of angels. He was born in Geneva, Switzerland, in 1712 and died in 1778. He never knew his mother nor the affection or interest of his father, or other relatives. This song still survives and has passed down through the ages, and almost every child in Christendom has heard the strains of 'Greenfield,' 'Rosseau's Dream,' and 'Sweet Affliction.'

146.title: New Hope
146.firstLine: Jesus, what shall I do to show
146.scriptureReference: "Greater love than this hath no man."—John 15:13
146.historicalNote: Professor A. M. Cagle lives at the present time (1908) in Alabama. See further sketch of him under the tune, 'New Jordan.'

147.title: Save, Mighty Lord
147.firstLine: Jesus, my all, to heav'n is gone,

musicAttribution.credit: J. A. and J. F. Wade

147.scriptureReference: "The Lord . . . was received up into heaven, and sat at the right hand of God."—Mark 16:19
147.historicalNote: John Cennick was born in 1718 and died in 1755. He was an English Moravian, and published the above words in 1743, twelve years before he died. The name of the song was, 'O Save.' We have changed it to, 'Save, Mighty Lord.' J. A. and J. F. Wade lived in South Carolina when they composed the above piece of music. They composed several other songs in the 'Social Harp,' published by John G. McCurry, in 1855. We can get no further trace of them. They were probably brothers.

148.title: Mary Blain
148.firstLine: Do not I love Thee, O my Lord?

musicAttribution.credit: G. B. Daniell and J. S. James (re-arr.)

148.scriptureReference: "We love him because he first loved us."—1 John 4:19
148.historicalNote: The air of 'Mary Blain' is an old melody of ante-bellum days. The notes were first applied to it by Henry F. Chandler in 1854. We have been unable to get any data about him in order to give a more extended sketch. He assisted John G. McCurry in compiling the 'Social Harp.' Mr. McCurry lived at Amandaville, Hart County, Ga. His book, the 'Social Harp,' was published in 1855. Philip Doddridge, the author of the words, was born in London in 1702. He was an English Congregationalist, and died in 1752. He spent most of his days as pastor in New Hampton. He was a man of wide influence and reputation, and the author of many hymns and poems.

149.title: Avon
149.firstLine: Planted in Christ, the living Vine,
149.historicalNote: Isaac Watts is the author of the above words. They appeared in the author's hymn book of 'Spiritual Songs' in 1707. The original title to the hymn was 'Godly Sorrow Arising from the Suffering of Christ.' In verse three the author wrote, 'When God the Maker Died.' Dr. Watts was one among the most extended and popular hymn writers of the English-speaking world. He was born 1673 and died 1748. He was an English Congregationalist minister. Hugh Wilson, the author of the music to the above hymn, was born 1764 and died 1824. He was a Scotchman, born in a Scotch village, and was a shoemaker by trade. The music of this hymn was composed some time in the eighteenth century.

150.title: Only Trust Him
150.firstLine: Come, ev'ry soul by sin oppressed,
150.scriptureReference: "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; . . . and ye shall find rest unto your souls."—Matt. 11:29
150.historicalNote: Rev. J. H. Stockton was a Methodist minister. He wrote the music about 1870, as also the words. This was one of the great favorites of Moody and Sankey. It was sung in many of their revival meetings in England and America, and is now placed in most of the standard hymn books of this country and many foreign countries.

151.title: Duke Street
151.firstLine: From all that dwell below the skies
151.scriptureReference: "O praise the Lord all ye nations; praise him all ye people."—Ps. 117:1
151.historicalNote: Little is known of John Hatton, who is credited by a number of histories as composing 'Duke Street.' The biographical index of the 'Angelical Hymnal' credits him as being the author of 'Duke Street.' He resided at Warrington, afterward at St. Helena, and then in Duke Street in the town of Windle. He composed several hymn tunes, and died 1793. He was a Presbyterian; and tradition says he was killed by being thrown from a stage coach. This is one of Isaac Watts' standard hymns, and is regarded by Robert Elson Thompson, S. T. D., in his 'National Hymn Book,' as being one of the up-to-date hymns of the American churches.

152.title: A Sister's Farewell
152.firstLine: Farewell, dear brothers, fare you well,
152.scriptureReference: "Suffer little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven. For in the resurrection they . . . are as the angels of God in heaven."—Matt. 19:14; 22:30
152.historicalNote: Professor A. J. McLendon, who is the author of the above tune and words, wrote the same in memory of Bertha B. Brantly, youngest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. D. Laminack. Professor McLendon, at this time (1909), resides in Carroll County, Ga. He has composed several tunes, and has successfully taught a number of singing schools. He is a member of the Chattahoochee Singing Convention, and for some time was its president. He helped to organize the United Sacred Harp Musical Association several years ago. He loves music, and often leads the great musical conventions of the country.

153t.title: Keller
153t.firstLine: My Christian friends to whom I speak
153t.scriptureReference: "For ye yourselves are taught of God to love one another."—1 Thess. 4:9
153t.historicalNote: Mrs. Denson is a fine singer and leader, and often attends the singing conventions with her husband, and engages in both singing and teaching. Her maiden name was Miss Burdett, and she comes from a musical family.

153b.title: Jasper
153b.firstLine: Great God, let all Thy tuneful pow'r

harmonizationAttribution.credit: Words re-arranged by T. J. Denson

153b.historicalNote: Professor T. J. Denson resides at this time (1909) in Winston County, Alabama. He has been singing ever since he was a small boy. He was taught music by his older brother, S. M. Denson. He has probably taught more singing schools and more people to sing than any teacher in Georgia or Alabama. No man lives who loves music more than Tom Denson, as he is usually called. He and his brother, S. M. Denson, have taught singing schools all over North Alabama and in several of the counties in Georgia. They have established a number of singing conventions in North Alabama. His father was a Methodist preacher, and was himself a musician. T. J. Denson and his brother, S. M. Denson, married the Misses Burdetts. Tom and his wife both lead the music in conventions and the great musical gatherings wherever they go. They have several children, some of whom are teachers and compose music. Professor and Mrs. Denson are members of the Missionary Baptist church. T. J. Denson is president of several singing conventions in Alabama. He has several tunes in this book, and has composed a great deal of music.

155.title: Liberty
155.firstLine: No more beneath the oppressive hand
155.scriptureReference: "Deliver me from the oppression of man."—Ps. 119:134
155.historicalNote: Stephen Jenks, of New Canaan, Conn., published the 'Delights of Harmony' in 1805. Twenty-six of the tunes in this book were composed by him, and the work was published by subscription. He removed to Thompson and died there in 1856. He was a ready composer.

156.title: Loving Kindness
156.firstLine: Awake, my soul, to joyful lays,
156.scriptureReference: "Joy unspeakable and full of glory."—1 Pet. 1:8
156.historicalNote: This hymn was composed by Samuel Medley, as his thanksgiving song, written soon after his conversion. He was a Baptist minister, born in England in 1738 and died in 1799. He wrote 230 hymns, some of the best are the following: 'Awake, My Soul, to Joyful Lays,' 'I Know That My Redeemer Lives,' 'O Could I Speak The Matchless Worth,' 'Mortals, Wake, With Angels Join.' See sketch of T. J. Denson, page 155.

157.title: Jesus Is A Friend
157.firstLine: Is your soul with sin distressed?
157.scriptureReference: "There is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother."—Prov. 18:24
157.historicalNote: Geo. B. Holsinger, the author of the above tune, is a teacher of wide reputation, author, and composer, and a great artist of music, was born in Pennsylvania in 1851. He was educated in the common schools of that State. He studied music in the normals wherever convenient under the instructions of the following eminent musicians: B. H. Everett, Dr. H. R. Palmer, A. J. Showalter, Geo. F. Root, and others. He taught music successfully twenty-five years, and composed a great deal of valuable music. For a long time he was connected with the music department of Bridgewater College. His home is in Virginia. Rev. E. A. Hoffman is a gifted poet and hymn writer. He has had a great deal to do with the music world, and is a minister, composer, and teacher of music. He is a Presbyterian, was born in Pennsylvania in 1839, and began his musical career in 1860, a year before his ministry. He has edited, composed, and compiled over forty song books. 'I Must Tell Jesus' is considered one of his best songs, and is used all over Christendom.

158.title: Logan
158.firstLine: The day is past and gone
158.historicalNote: John Leland was a Baptist minister, born in 1754 and died in 1844. See sketch on pages 94 and 106. See also sketch of T. J. Denson, page 155.

159.title: Love
159.firstLine: O for a closer walk with God,
159.historicalNote: William Cowper was born in 1739 and died in 1800. He was one of the most beloved of English poets. This suffering man was also a true Christian and died in faith of salvation through the atonement of Jesus Christ. See full sketch of Mr. Cowper under tune 'New York' page three. See sketch of Professor Denson on page 155.

160.title: Seek The Lord
160.firstLine: Seek ye the Lord, seek ye the Lord,
160.historicalNote: Professor T. J. Denson, the author of this tune, lives in Winston County, Alabama. See further sketch of him on page 130.

161.title: Coming To The Cross
161.firstLine: I am coming to the cross
161.scriptureReference: "Let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me."—Mark 8:34
161.historicalNote: The above hymn was written in Brooklyn, N. Y., while Mr. McDonald was pastor in that city. The hymn was first sung at a national camp-meeting, held in Hampton, Mass., in 1870. It has been translated into many languages, and sung all around the globe. The words were inseparably attached to Mr. Fischer's tune, 'I Am Coming To The Cross.' The name has been changed several times, as follows: 'I Am Trusting, Lord, In Thee,' 'I Am Trusting, Lord,' and other names. We have given it the name, 'Coming To The Cross.' Wm. G. Fischer was born in Baltimore, Md., in 1835. He wrote many sweet melodies, and has held many positions which required the best musicians of the country to occupy. Some of his best compositions are: 'I Love To Tell The Story,' 'Whiter Than Snow,' 'The Rock That Is Higher Than I,' and many others.

162.title: The Lifeboat
162.firstLine: We are floating down the stream of time

textAttribution.credit: A. N. and M. M. Brahan

musicAttribution.credit: T. J. Denson, S. M. Denson

162.scriptureReference: "Lord make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is, that I may know how frail I am."—Ps. 39:4
162.historicalNote: See sketch of T. J. Denson on page 155, and also of S. M. Denson on page 130. Professor John R. Bryant is the author of the original air of this tune. It is presented now as written by S. M. and T. J. Denson.

163.title: Bound For Canaan
163.firstLine: O when shall I see Jesus,
163.scriptureReference: "Ye see him not, yet believing ye rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory."—1 Pet. 1:8
163.historicalNote: The original name of this song was 'Evening Song.' Rev. John Leland was born in 1754 and died in 1844. He was a Baptist preacher. In 1801 he took a preaching tour from his home in Massachusetts to Washington with his Cheshire cheese, and made his name national on account of that trip. He wrote his own hymns. He composed the hymn, 'The Day is Passed and Gone, The Evening Shades Appear.' The farmers of Cheshire, for whom he was pastor, conceived the idea of sending the biggest cheese in America to President Jefferson. Mr. Leland offered to go to Washington with an ox team with it, and preach all along the way, which he did. The cheese weighed 1,450 pounds. He died with bright hopes of rest in the glory world. E. J. King made material changes in the tune, and re-arranged it about the year 1846. He prepared it for the 'Sacred Harp.' See sketch on page 55.

164.title: Sweet Home
164.firstLine: 'Mid scenes of confusion and creature complaints
164.scriptureReference: "We rejoice by faith in hope of the glory of God."—Rom. 5:2
164.historicalNote: 'Sweet Home,' according to the older histories, was composed by John Howard Payne, being one of the airs of his opera, 'Clari, the Maid of Milan,' used by him in London in 1823. It is asserted by Mackey, an English poet, that Sir Henry Bishop, an eminent musician, composed the music, and that the air of this tune was of Sicilian nationality. It is certain, however, that John Howard Payne was the author of the words, ''Mid scenes of confusion, etc.' He was an American, born in New York in 1791. He was a singer of great ability, and wrote many theatrical tunes. It is claimed by some, and it seems on good authority, that he wrote the music of 'Sweet Home' in 1823, as well as the words, when he was himself homeless, without friends or money, and among strangers, resting, temporarily, in an attic in Paris. His fortune after this time, however, improved, and he was appointed by the United States Government as Consul to Tunis, where he died in 1852. He began his usefulness as a clerk when 13 years of age, and edited a newspaper at that age in New York. He entered the theater in 1809, after which time he visited, in that capacity, Boston, Philadelphia, and Baltimore. In 1813 he carried his theatrical troupe to England, and first appeared at Drury Lane Theater. The publishers of 'Sweet Home' cleared 2,000 guineas in two years. In 1832 more than 100,000 copies had been sold. In 1826-27 he edited a London periodical, 'The Opera Glass.' Returned to America in 1832, and in 1841 he represented his country as consul. In 1851 he was re-appointed. The United States has erected a monument over his remains at the Cemetery St. George, Tunis, and a bust has also been placed in Prospect Park, Brooklyn.

165.title: Yield Not To Temptation
165.firstLine: Yield not to temptation, for yielding is sin,
165.historicalNote: Dr. H. R. Palmer was born in New York State in 1834. His father and mother were excellent musicians, and his early training was exceptionally good. He was an author, composer, director, lecturer, and publisher of music, and was an exceptionally fine scholar. His musical attainments were second to none in the country. He received the degree, Mus. Doc., from the University of Chicago in 1883. In composing and rendering music he exemplified the highest degree of genius. 'Yield not to Temptation,' is said to be one of his best sacred tunes. He wrote 'Theory of Music,' 'Piano Primer,' 'Dictionary of Musical Terms,' 'Dictionary of Music and Musicians,' and many other standard works. He died in New York in 1908. (Note: the printed page numbers the three surviving stanzas 1, 2, and 5, skipping 3 and 4 as printed.)

166.title: Funeral Anthem
166.firstLine: I heard a great voice from heav'n saying unto me
166.historicalNote: The words in the above piece of music are taken from Rev. 14:13. William Billings was born in Boston in 1746 and died there in 1800. He is buried in the old Granary burying ground in the city of his birth. He was self-taught in music. He was criticised by many musicians and music writers, and while he did not believe so much in rules, he wrote some very fine music. His first book was, 'New England Psalm Singer,' the next was called 'Billing's Best.' He published several other books and wrote and composed many national tunes that stirred the people of the United States. Many of his tunes still remain in the note and hymn books of the different churches. 'Easter Anthems,' 'Heavenly Vision,' 'Rose of Sharon,' and many other anthems, known to many people of the South, were composed by him.

167.title: The Blind Girl
167.firstLine: Mother, they say the stars are bright,

textAttribution.credit: J. M. and J. C. Brown

musicAttribution.credit: J. M. and J. C. Brown

168t.title: Duke
168t.firstLine: Mixtures of joy and sorrow, I daily do pass thro',
168t.scriptureReference: "Count it all joy when ye fall into diverse temptations; knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience."—James 1:2,3
168t.historicalNote: The above tune was composed by Professor McWhorter in honor of 'Welcome Duke.' For further sketch of Professor McWhorter see tune 'Kerr,' on page 169 in this book. His present address is Fruit Hurst, Alabama. (Respectfully inscribed in honor of 'Welcome Duke.')

168b.title: Kerr
168b.historicalNote: The words to the above tune are taken from Floyd's 'Primitive Hymn Book,' and are connected with the tune, 'Endless Distress,' by Rev. Edmund Dumas. The above tune, 'Kerr,' was composed by Professor M. F. McWhorter in memory of his friend, A. A. Kerr. Mr. McWhorter resides at the present time in Cleburne County, Alabama. He has been engaged in the teaching of music in Alabama and Georgia for twenty five years, and is well up in music—a fine teacher, leader, singer, and composer. He is president of the Cleburne County Singing Convention, and a member of all the singing societies in his section. He is on the committee to revise the 'Sacred Harp,' and helped to organize the United Sacred Harp Musical Association. (Written January 16, 1909, in honor of A. A. Kerr.)

169.title: Eternal Are Thy Mercies
169.firstLine: From all that dwell below the skies,
169.scriptureReference: "The earth, O Lord, is full of thy mercy."—Ps. 119:64
169.historicalNote: Mr. McWhorter lives in Atlanta at this time (1909). He is a son of Professor M. F. McWhorter of Fruithurst, Ala. His people are all musical, and he is a fine leader and singer. He is a young man, twenty years old, and just beginning to compose and write music. The tunes in this book bearing his name are some of his first efforts. The words in this tune are taken from 'Schenectady,' in the 'Sacred Harp.'

170.title: At The Saviour's Right Hand
170.firstLine: In the day of all days, when the world shall be judged,
170.scriptureReference: "He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth much fruit."—John 15:5
170.historicalNote: See history of George Holsinger under tune of 'Jesus Is a Friend.' Much more could be said commending him than set out under that tune. E. R. Latta was a musician of considerable experience, and wrote the above hymn, as well as many others. He was an expert musician, hymn and poetry writer.

171.title: Happy Land
171.firstLine: There is a happy land, far, far away,
171.scriptureReference: "Then shall every man have the praise of God."—1 Cor. 4:5
171.historicalNote: It is thought that Leonard P. Breedlove made some changes in the treble of the music, and re-arranged the chorus. The air of 'Happy Land' came from the Hindoos, and is being hummed in the Pagan temple, and has been sung all over the world wherever missionaries have roamed. The musician, Samuel Wesley, some time in 1840, tried to substitute another melody to these lines, but 'There is a happy land' seemed to carry forth its own name, and cannot be supplanted by another melody.

172.title: Rescue The Perishing
172.firstLine: Rescue the perishing, Care for the dying,
172.scriptureReference: "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him."—Heb. 7:25
172.historicalNote: Fanny J. Crosby is known as the blind poet, having written over six thousand hymns. She became blind when six weeks old. See further history of her under tune, 'Pass Me Not.' W. H. Doane was born in Connecticut in 1832, and was educated at Woodstock, Conn. He belongs to the Baptist church. He wrote his first song in 1848, and was said to have dedicated it to his schoolmates. His first book was published in 1862, another in 1864. In 1867, it is claimed, he sold over three hundred thousand copies. Since then he has composed many other pieces which have obtained great popularity. He is one of the best known American composers who have made great success in the musical world.

173.title: Go Ye Forth And Labor
173.firstLine: Go ye forth and labor In the field away
173.historicalNote: Professor J. B. Vaughan, author, composer, teacher, and publisher, was born in 1860. He is practically self-taught in music. His first effort as an author was in assisting Professor A. J. Showalter in publishing 'Glad Tidings,' in 1884. The A. J. Showalter Company published perhaps his first book, 'Our Wreath,' since which time he has published his own music, and has written and compiled about twenty books. He still continues to write and compose music. Some of his favorite books are: 'Windows of Heaven,' 'Promised Day,' and several others. Professor Vaughan is a ready writer, and possesses a strong musical talent. His tunes present an individuality which few composers possess. He has a fine voice, and is a splendid director and leader of large choruses, classes, and musical gatherings. He is located at Athens, Ga.

174.title: Standing On The Promises
174.firstLine: Standing on the promises of Christ my King
174.scriptureReference: "He hath promised us eternal life."—1 John 2:25
174.historicalNote: The author of this hymn is an evangelist and resides in the State of California. He has composed several other good tunes and hymns.

175.title: Let Us Go Forth
175.firstLine: Silent, like men in solemn haste,
175.scriptureReference: "He that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live."—John 11:25
175.historicalNote: See sketch of J. C. Brown on page 129 under 'New Rock of Ages.'

176.title: Jesus Saves
176.firstLine: We have heard the joyful sound, Jesus saves,
176.scriptureReference: "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved."—Acts 16:31
176.historicalNote: Professor Wm. J. Kirkpatrick is a teacher and composer of wide reputation. He was born February 22, 1838. He joined the Methodist church when 17 years of age, and after which he devoted his time to sacred music. He had the best instructors, and has composed many hymns, tunes, and sweet melodies. His first book was 'Devotional Melodies.' He has been engaged a great deal of the time in manufacturing industry. His name is a household word in nearly all of the Christian families of the United States, and he has music in all the leading tune books. He is a man of great power and influence.

177.title: Rolling On
177.firstLine: The time is swiftly rolling on, rolling on, rolling on,
177.historicalNote: William H. Guthery composed the above tune, and re-arranged the words in 1908. He lives in North Alabama, and attends all the leading musical gatherings, conventions and societies in that section of the country. He is a fine singer and a dear lover of music.

178.title: Eternity
178.firstLine: Did Jesus die that we might live?
178.scriptureReference: "To obtain salvation with eternal glory."—2 Tim. 2:10.
178.historicalNote: William H. Guthery composed the above tune and hymn. He belongs to the Cullman County (Alabama) Convention, as well as to several other musical associations in North Alabama, and attends all the leading musical associations in his section. He has composed several tunes and hymns, and is engaged in extending the art and science over the country where he lives. He has many friends among musical people.

179.title: Heavenly Gates
179.scriptureReference: "Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lifted up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in."—Ps. 24:7.
179.historicalNote: NOTE.—If the Coda be sung the last note of the tune must be omitted, and the small note before the Coda takes its place. The hymn of the above tune is based on Psalm 24. The hymn was written, or, at least, partly written, from the best sources we can gather, by Miss Harriet L. Auber. She was born in London in 1773 and died there in 1862. She was an English lady, and published a book of poems, entitled 'Spirit of the Psalms.' All her hymns are considered first class, and received the endorsement of Duffield, and also of Brown and Butterworth. The above and foregoing tunes were re-arranged by R. J. DeLay and J. S. James. The original author we have been unable to find. Its original name was 'Eton,' and has been changed in this book to 'Heavenly Gates.' Professor R. J. DeLay resides at this time (1909) in Gwinnett County, Ga. He has composed several tunes heretofore, and if he has had them published it is unknown to us. He is a fine leader and director of music, and attends the musical conventions and other gatherings, and is especially fond of the old sacred songs. He has a strong, smooth tenor voice, and can reach the highest notes or strains without inconvenience. No one loves sacred songs better than he. Professor DeLay is one of the original promoters of the United Sacred Harp Musical Association, and one of the original promoters of the Sacred Harp class in Atlanta.

180.title: Blessed Home
180.firstLine: O think of a home over there,
180.scriptureReference: "And shewed me that great city, the holy Jerusalem, descending out of heaven from God."—Rev. 21:10.
180.historicalNote: Dr. W. C. D. Huntingdon was born in 1838. He resides in Nebraska, and is a Methodist minister. See sketch of him on page 100. There are two tunes in this volume from Professor Showalter. The above, 'Blessed Home,' which he almost made new in 1905. The other tune on page 32, 'Leaning on the Everlasting Arms,' for want of space, we did not give the history of Professor Showalter in connection with 'Leaning on the Everlasting Arms,' for this tune is the equal, if not the greatest, in popularity of any tune ever composed by this gifted musician. Professor A. J. Showalter, teacher, author, editor and publisher, was born in Rockingham County, Va., in 1858. He spent his early childhood in the Old Dominion, in the Shenandoah Valley. His father, John A. Showalter, was a native Virginian, and his mother, Susannah (Miller) Showalter, traces her ancestry to Germany. They were both musical. His father was a music teacher, and was considered first-class in the profession. He was a man of high standing, Christian character, and strong religious convictions. Professor Showalter received his training in private schools taught by his father and others. He has had the very best musical education and instruction that was possible to obtain from the musical conservatories and normal schools in the United States. After completing his studies and establishing his reputation as a teacher, in 1895, he went abroad and studied the methods of the music teachers and schools in England, France and Germany. When only 14 years of age he began his career as a teacher, by assisting his father. He taught singing schools in many counties in Virginia and West Virginia, since which time he moved to Georgia and settled in Dalton, where he now resides, 1909. For the last 20 years or more, he has taught normal schools in almost every Southern State. Thousands of people have received instructions in his normals and other musical gatherings. The fact is, his reputation as a music teacher in all branches, and especially in sacred music, extends all over the United States. He has composed some of the best sacred music now used in all Christian branches of the Church, and especially in the South. He has composed and compiled over sixty-five different music books. He is president of the A. J. Showalter Publishing Co., Dalton, Ga. In connection with this, he publishes a music journal. He has composed and published more sacred tunes than any other musician in the Southern States. The fact is, he is one of the largest contributors to the advancement of art and science of music who has resided in this country since it was first founded. He continues to teach normal schools and compose music, which requires his entire time. He is a liberal-spirited man, has done almost more than any other individual south of the Mason and Dixon line, for the cause of music. The music people regardless of notation or class, love him everywhere. He was the director and manager of the largest gathering of singers that has ever met in the Southern States, at the all-day singing at the State Fair, in Atlanta, Ga., 1905, where five thousand voices responded to his call, and left a memorable day in the history of gospel songs. Professor Showalter is an Elder in the Presbyterian church and stands high in the councils of his denomination. He is extremely liberal to all denominations, and a strong supporter of the Christian people everywhere. The tune, 'Leaning on the Everlasting Arms,' has met the appreciation of nearly every Christian home in the south, as well as to spread its wings over countries wherever Christianity is preached and gospel songs sung. 'Blessed Home,' as arranged by Professor Showalter, is another melody that is like unto 'Leaning on the Everlasting Arms.' It is sung, played, and enjoyed by all Christian people.

182.title: Resurrected
182.firstLine: My father's gone to view that land,
182.scriptureReference: "And they ascended up to heaven in a cloud."—Rev. 11:12.
182.historicalNote: The words of this hymn were arranged by Professor Denson in 1908, and applied to the music composed at the same date. See sketch of him on page 130. * Use mother, brother, and sister for other verses.

184t.historicalNote: Rev. E. A. Hoffman, the author of the above music, was born in 1839. He was educated in the public schools of Philadelphia, and began preaching in 1861. He is a Presbyterian. His first musical composition was published in 1860, and his first music book appeared 1868, since which time he has edited and assisted in compiling over forty different song books. Many of his songs appear in books and are popular with the people. He is not a fine musician but a minister of distinction.

184b.title: Restoration
184b.firstLine: Come, thou Fount of ev'ry blessing,
